newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Opposition seeks more Western pressure on Milosevic.
newsitem.headline: Opposition seeks more Western pressure on Milosevic.

text.p: A Serbian opposition leader called on the West on Friday to step up pressure for democratic change after President Slobodan Milosevic issued a statement which ignored the crux of the nine-week political crisis.
Vuk Draskovic, one of three leaders of the Zajedno (Together) coalition, told Reuters in an interview that international pressure so far had been inadequate.
He said the major powers had a duty to ensure Milosevic respected the commitments to foster democracy he made in the 1995 Bosnian peace accord and should be further isolated.
"I am not quite satisfied with international pressure because that pressure is not very effective," he said, speaking during a visit to Rome with his two coalition co-leaders.

Milosevic, in a statement issued on Thursday night to the state-run news agency Tanjug, alluded to the protests over the annulment of opposition wins in municipal elections in November without saying whether these victories should be reinstated.

Ignoring the clamour for democratic change, he said "political confrontations" were damaging the interests of Serbian-led federal Yugoslavia and that disputes should be solved in a "constructive and democratic" manner.
Tens of thousands of opposition supporters have demonstrated almost daily in protest at the alleged election-rigging in 14 Serbian cities, bringing normal life to a halt.
Electoral commissions on Tuesday acknowledged "preliminary results" showing that the opposition bloc had won Belgrade and Nis, Serbia's two biggest cities.
But hardliners in Milosevic's Socialist Party vowed to appeal against those decisions, suggesting the strongman leader had not sanctioned the concessions himself.
Milosevic also set his sights on a cabinet shuffle, apparently to purge unpopular ministers linked to corruption and mismanagement of Yugoslavia's shambolic state-run economy.

But he skirted the issue at the heart of Serbia's political crisis, despite a strong appeal from the 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe hours earlier for the opposition election wins to be respected.

Shortly after the OSCE appeal, the European Parliament in Strasbourg passed a resolution saying the European Union and its individual member countries should freeze relations with Serbia until democracy has been established there.

Draskovic, in Rome for talks with the Italian government, stopped short of calling for a resumption of international economic sanctions against Serbia that were lifted in 1996 as a reward for peace in Bosnia.

"Against Milosevic and his mafia, yes. (But) not against our state and people because the people are suffering too much. The biggest sanction...against Serbia is Mr Milosevic and his dictatorship," Draskovic said.
Draskovic said recognition of Zajedno's election triumphs was the "condition of all conditions" for ending the mass street protests that have challenged effective one-party rule for the first time.

Draskovic, who along with co-opposition leaders Zoran Djindjic and Vesna Pesic was meeting Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, said Milosevic had lost majority support in Serbia and was acting like a dictator.
"I am quite sure this is the last year of Milosevic's rule in Serbia. Very many people are against Milosevic. The majority of people are against Milosevic."
It was not clear what concrete steps on the Serbian crisis might emerge from Zajedno's talks in Italy, which some diplomats said looked like a fence-mending exercise by Rome.

Dini claimed credit last month for obtaining consent from Milosevic during talks in Belgrade to allow an OSCE mission led by former Spanish prime minister Felipe Gonzalez to visit Serbia and investigate the polls. It found the opposition won.
But Dini angered Zajedno during the same visit when he said that reinstatement of the disputed election results was not "on the cards" as a basis for dialogue with Milosevic.
